clue.text: In the course of card game, putting in pound

indicators.note: to put something in is to insert it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: whist is a trick-taking card game for four
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone slips a pound into the kitty partway through a hand of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: The pound symbol £ is a stylised L, from libra; that letter sits inside the game WHIST to give WHILST.
explanation.definitionFit: Whilst is a British conjunction meaning during the time that, just as one thing happens over the period of another.

clue.text: Goals I have presented in articles

indicators.note: something presented in a case or wrapping is enclosed by it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: articles in the sense of things or items
the contraction I've, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A speaker announces the aims they have set out across a series of written pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests newspaper pieces or grammatical a and the, but here it means things or items.
explanation.definitionFit: Objectives are aims or targets someone works towards, a close synonym for goals in planning or sport.

clue.text: Ten fish shot under the surface

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten
a ray is a flat cartilaginous fish

explanation.surface: Someone fires at a shoal of ten fish below the water line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like gunfire at fish in the water; it is a photograph, and 'under the surface' is what that picture reveals inside the body.
explanation.definitionFit: An X-ray is a medical image that shows bones and organs beneath the skin, so a picture of what lies within.

clue.text: Wed heartless lady to a man

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle letters are cut out, leaving only the two ends

parts.note: wed as a past participle: joined, made one
the word with its central letters removed

explanation.surface: An instruction to marry a woman, who has no heart, off to some man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To a man' sounds like the groom in a wedding, but it is an idiom meaning everyone without exception.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting all together as one body is what the idiom 'to a man' describes: unanimously, with nobody dissenting.

clue.text: Characters collectively gaining height on mountain with support

indicators.note: to gain something is to add it on, so a piece is attached to the end of another
one thing on another follows it here, so the earlier-named piece comes second

parts.note: an alp is a high mountain, as in the Alps
H is the standard abbreviation for height
to abet is to help or back someone

explanation.surface: A band of people climbing a peak together, getting higher with the help of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like people in a story or climbers; it means letters. The mountain gains H, then the support follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The full set of letters used to write a language, taken as one group, is its alphabet.

clue.text: Inspect fine ring in girlfriend's possession

indicators.note: being in something means being enclosed by it, so these letters go inside
what is in someone's possession is held by them, so the outer piece holds the inner

parts.note: a lover is a romantic partner
O is ring-shaped
OK means fine, all right

explanation.surface: Someone examines a good-quality ring that the girlfriend has been given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine ring' reads as a quality piece of jewellery, but the two words are separate pieces, taken in reverse order inside the partner.
explanation.definitionFit: To look over a document or car is to examine it, usually quickly, so it matches inspect as a verb.

clue.text: Don't disregard awful UFO attack once

indicators.note: something awful is in a terrible state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the thirteen letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A warning not to dismiss a terrible alien assault from the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' looks like it dates the attack, but it is just more letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To take account of something is to consider it rather than ignore it, the positive form of not disregarding.

clue.text: English chap monarch brought back to bestow another title on

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a chap is a man
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A restored king returns to give an Englishman a new honour.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, a standard crossword monarch; together with the other pieces it reads backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To rename something is to give it a different name, and a title is simply a name for a person or thing.

clue.text: People joining university that provides information about courses

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the thing that does this

parts.note: men as people in general
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: New students enrol at a university that publishes details of its degree programmes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' sounds academic beside 'university', but means the stages of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant's menu lists the dishes for each stage of a meal, such as starter, main and dessert.

clue.text: Essay, a piece of fiction that's number one in the field

parts.note: an essay is an attempt, a go
taken as written
a lie is an invented story

explanation.surface: A school essay or short story judged the best of its kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay' means a written piece in the surface but an attempt in the wordplay. The definition plays on the goalkeeper's shirt number.
explanation.definitionFit: In football and hockey the goalkeeper traditionally wears shirt number 1, so is literally the number one on the pitch.

clue.text: Piano piece's sound quality is what everything depends on

parts.note: a key is one piece of a piano, with the possessive 's
tone is the quality of a sound

explanation.surface: The tonal quality of a piano composition is the thing that matters most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano piece' reads as a composition; it is a component of the instrument, a key.
explanation.definitionFit: A keystone is the central wedge at the top of an arch that holds the other stones, so figuratively the crucial support.

clue.text: Chemist, short of cash, began using computer

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the final letter is lopped off

parts.note: Boots is a UK chain of pharmacies, here without its last letter
strapped for cash means hard up; 'short' also serves this sense

explanation.surface: A broke scientist starts working with a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: Chemist is the British word for a pharmacy, and Boots is the best-known high-street one. 'Short' does double duty, trimming the shop and joining 'of cash' to mean hard up.
explanation.definitionFit: To bootstrap a computer is to start it up by loading its operating system, now usually shortened to booting.

clue.text: As it is, chop bananas and nuts

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

parts.note: the ten letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A kitchen instruction: leave things as they are, cut up the bananas and the nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' sits among food words as a fruit to chop, but it is slang for crazy and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Pistachios are green-kernelled edible seeds from a Middle Eastern tree, commonly eaten and sold as nuts.

clue.text: Envisaged developments in a score being composed

indicators.note: composing means putting together, so the letters are assembled in a new arrangement

parts.note: the eight letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A composer imagines how the themes will develop within a musical score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developments' and 'score' sound musical; the score is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A scenario is an imagined sequence of future events, the way a situation might plausibly unfold.

clue.text: Frenchman or Englishwoman, so-called?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a common French man's first name
second meaning: a woman's first name in English

explanation.walkthrough: 'So-called' tells you both are names: the same spelling is male in French and female in English.
explanation.definitionFit: The French masculine name, equivalent to John, is spelt identically to the English feminine name, as in Jean Brodie.

clue.text: Showing effects of swelling, unusually loud in organ

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it

parts.note: the nose is the organ of smell

indicators.note: done in an unusual way, so the letters come out in a different order

parts.note: the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A swollen organ, perhaps in the ear or throat, makes an unusually loud noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' with 'loud' suggests music; it is a body part, the NOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nodulose means covered in nodules, the small lumps or knots that swelling produces in tissue or plants.

clue.text: Weaknesses in carpenters' tools

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bad habits or moral failings
second meaning: clamps for holding work steady, usually spelt vise in the US

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests faults in a set of tools; the two parts are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both moral failings or bad habits and workbench clamps that grip wood while it is cut.

clue.text: Rabbit sounding like domesticated animal

indicators.note: these words compare how something is said, not how it is spelt

parts.note: the yak is a Himalayan ox kept as livestock

explanation.surface: A pet bunny that makes noises like a farm animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' looks like the animal but is British slang for chatter, from rhyming slang rabbit and pork, talk.
explanation.definitionFit: To rabbit on is British informal for talking at length, just as to yack is to chatter idly.

clue.text: Debates ain't so stupid if appropriately organised

indicators.note: organising things arranges them properly, so these letters are set into the right order

parts.note: the twelve letters, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Arguments are not so foolish once they are properly structured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupid' looks like the signal to rearrange, but it is part of the letters; the signal is the closing phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Disputations are formal arguments or discussions on a contested point, much like academic debates.

clue.text: Bad influence? Too right!

parts.note: ill as in bad, harmful
to have a say is to have influence

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether another is a bad influence, and gets emphatic agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The question and reply look like a conversation; the question is the wordplay and the reply the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal exclamations of strong agreement: too right is Australian and British, I'll say is the same emphatic yes.

clue.text: Final letter heard on radio is one from Africa

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the radio code word for the last letter, Z
second meaning: a member of a southern African people

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' is not a sound-alike signal here; it points to the spelling alphabet used over radio, where each letter has a code word.
explanation.definitionFit: The NATO phonetic alphabet ends with this code word for Z, and the Zulu are a large nation of South Africa.

clue.text: Least straight — is deceptive, in short

indicators.note: being in something means being enclosed by it

parts.note: curt means short, abrupt in manner
someone who lies is being deceptive

explanation.surface: The least honest person is the most deceptive, put briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' looks like a phrase meaning briefly, but splits into the container signal and the word CURT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something most curly has the most twists and bends, which makes it the furthest from being straight.

clue.text: Mark's replacement in amateur operatics

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

parts.note: found across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: An understudy named Mark is replaced in an amateur stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a person's name but is the old German currency, the Deutschmark.
explanation.definitionFit: Germany's Deutschmark was withdrawn in 2002 when the single European currency took its place.

clue.text: Legal term starts off hearing, in legal action regarding youth

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, which are the ones taken

parts.words: hearing, in legal action regarding youth
parts.note: the opening letter of each of the six words

explanation.surface: A juvenile court case opens with a hearing at the start of a legal term.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal language makes this read as a court report; 'starts off' just takes word beginnings.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilary term is the sitting of the English courts and Oxford University running from January to around Easter.

clue.text: In the role of queen, when centrally placed, revealing heavenly body

indicators.note: placed in the centre means set into the middle of the other letters

parts.note: qua is Latin for in the capacity of
R for Regina, queen
as meaning while, when

explanation.surface: An actor cast as a queen, standing centre stage, is revealed as a star.
explanation.walkthrough: QUA is a Latin word used in English for 'in the capacity of'. 'Queen' wants to be QU or ER; here it is R, and AS goes into the middle of QUAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A quasar is an extremely bright, distant galactic nucleus, an astronomical object in the sky.

clue.text: Totally how the first answer goes, or all them, initially
